title: That’s so primary school
author: Shaun Brien
summary: Shaun Brien teaches at a senior secondary college in Victoria and pushes back on the staff assumption that Year 10 to 12 students are mature, autonomous learners who need no explicit teaching. Drawing on the biologically primary versus secondary knowledge distinction, he argues that school content must be taught, not caught, and that the common senior-school defaults (long lecturing, or setting students loose to research with AI) fail. He answers the frequent objection that checking-for-understanding routines are "so primary school" by presenting six such strategies he uses with older students. These are choral response, mini whiteboards, think/pair/share, attention signals, routines, and sentence stems or cloze tasks. For each he explains the mechanism, usually in terms of working memory, cognitive load or visible thinking. His closing claim is that these methods take little planning, save marking and intervention time, and that best practice does not discriminate by age.
points: Senior teachers often assume older students are autonomous learners, but the author argues that content is biologically secondary and must be explicitly taught and sequenced at any age.
Choral response and mini whiteboards give a check for understanding that students cannot opt out of, which suits peak-passive-disengagement teenagers.
Rock-solid routines, such as a Do Now on entry and a countdown before holding up whiteboards, remove transition time and lower cognitive load.
Attention signals with pens down and screens off matter because information that never reaches working memory cannot reach long-term memory.
Sentence stems and cloze tasks let teachers assess knowledge in classes with very wide literacy ranges without penalising weak writers.
quotes: Despite some learning being biologically primary (speaking, facial recognition etc), content taught in schools is biologically secondary. Therefore, it isn’t innate to them. It is artificially created. Knowledge which must be taught, not caught.
It shouldn’t be about wanting to learn. Why would they want to learn? It is our job to teach them.

When working with mini whiteboards it is incredibly important that you set routines which are rock solid. Without routines around how the students get their whiteboard when they come into class, how they show their work and where they put their whiteboard during instruction, you could be left with 25 students doodling not only wasting time but wasting your precious ink.
Often in a senior school we fall into the habit of stating “there just isn’t enough time, we need to plough through the content”. There’s always time. Slow is smooth and smooth is fast.

Having students’ full attention is the only way to guarantee that we can optimize students’ working memory so we can make learning stick. If the knowledge never makes it into the students’ working memory, then it doesn’t stand a chance making it into long term memory and therefore learning hasn’t happened.

The cognitive load of choosing where to start is insanely overwhelming. By providing sentence starters and gaps to fill student understanding of the knowledge is able to be quickly assessed without penalizing students for their ability to write.
It’s prime time we started implementing more of the incredible strategies our primary colleagues use day in and out because best practice doesn’t discriminate.
